stories.title: Teenager who died in Cork stabbing named locally
stories.summary: The 18-year-old who died after he was stabbed on the street in Cork yesterday has been named locally as Adam McSweeney from Glanmire. Mr McSweeney was on the Lower Glanmire Road, outside Kent railway station in Cork, when he became involved in an exchange with another group of teenagers. Mr McSweeney was stabbed and was critically injured, while the other teenagers fled the scene. He was taken to Cork University Hospital (CUH), where doctors fought for more than two hours to save his life, but he was pronounced dead at 4.15pm. The area where the fight occurred has been sealed off by gardaí for a technical examination. CCTV is being gathered from the area and detectives are interviewing witnesses. No weapon has been recovered.

stories.title: Entangled minke whale found dead on Donegal beach
stories.summary: A dead minke whale stranded on a beach on the Fanad Peninsula appeared to have been entangled in the lines of a fishing post, according to the Irish Whale and Dolphin Group (IWDG). The pectoral fins and head of the five-metre male whale were entangled in ropes, with two unmarked buoys still attached. The stranded whale was discovered by a walker on Baile Uí Thiarnáin beach, Co Donegal yesterday. The walker then notified the IWDG. The group said the minke whale had been dead for some time and was most likely entangled in the groundlines of pots. A 2022 Scottish paper on entangled whales found that approximately 30 minke and six humpback whales were entangled annually in the Scottish creel fisheries. IWDG Project Officer, Data Scientist Emilie De Loose said the whale populations of Scotland and Ireland overlap greatly, noting the similarities in the pot fishing industries.

stories.title: Nvidia chair dismisses idea of rehiring Huang
stories.summary: Nvidia board Chairman Harvey Jones opened a conference call with investors last night by saying the AI chip company would not rehire co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO and would not take questions about his departure. Coming on top of strong results, Jones' comments were a forceful response to a movement to bring back Huang, who stepped down last week. With Huang gone, investors are eager for clues about Nvidia's future and strategy, from its commitments of billions of dollars to cloud providers, suppliers and AI startups to who will ultimately lead the world's most valuable chipmaker. Jones said the board had hired executive search firm Heidrick & Struggles to help find a new CEO. "We want to install the CEO, the permanent CEO, as quickly as possible, but we won't expedite the CEO before finding exactly the right person," he added. He was joined on the call by interim CEO Colette Kress, who is also finance chief, and engineer Ian Buck, the vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing.

stories.title: Frawley repaying the faith as Springboks rematch looms
stories.summary: In a week of many talking points, it's easy to forget that Ireland v South Africa is a fixture often filled with drama. One man who has been at the centre of that is Ciarán Frawley. Back in 2024, he was seen as the main challenger to Jack Crowley, as Ireland’s number ten. However, starting berths with Leinster were limited, and there was the added setback of two late drop goal misses in the European final defeat to Toulouse. Come July, memories of the Tottenham Hotspur Stadium were banished as he helped Ireland to an historic win in Durban. The Skerries native kicked two last-gasp drop goals as Ireland stunned the world champions at the death. Those memories will be invaluable if Ireland are to repeat the trick on Saturday. "To win big games you need to tick all those boxes", the utility back told reporters on Monday. "We know South Africa are coming here after last weekend, the emotion they’re going to be going after, the way the game went against France, take that out on us.
stories.rssSummary: The last time Ireland defeated South Africa, Ciarán Frawley was the man of the hour. Now, after a strong start to the season with Connacht, he looks set to play a major role in the latest test between the nations.

stories.title: Island of Imagination: Oisín Fagan & Roisín O'Donnell
stories.summary: In The Island of Imagination, Laureate for Irish Fiction Éilís Ní Dhuibhne delves into contemporary Irish fiction on a journey of exploration to highlight literature emanating from every county in Ireland. In this series of in-conversation events, she speaks to some of our best contemporary literary fiction writers about their novels and short stories and their writing lives and ponders the question 'What makes a good story?'. In this episode, Éilís talks to novelists Oisín Fagan and Roisín O’Donnell about their respective novels Eden’s Shore and Nesting - watch their conversation above. This event was recorded at Trim Library and Swift Cultural Centre, with thanks to Meath Libraries. The Island of Imagination is an initiative of the Arts Council and the Laureate for Irish Fiction. stories.title: Joanne McNally defends appearing on Jimmy Fallon show
stories.summary: Joanne McNally has hit back at criticism over her decision to appear on The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon following Conor McGregor's appearance on the programme. The 43-year-old comedian, known for her bold and confessional style, received a standing ovation after performing a stand-up set on the US chat show last month. However, McNally revealed she faced criticism from female fans online for not boycotting the programme following Irish UFC fighter McGregor’s appearance in June. "I think the reason the Jimmy Fallon appearance became a much bigger deal than I expected was because, I don’t know if you’re aware, but some women on TikTok were saying I shouldn’t go on the show because they had Conor McGregor on as a guest," the Irish comedian told the Press Association. "I clapped back and said that if every woman missed out on an opportunity on a show because it had a bad man on the couch, there would be no women working." She added: "I think that got a bit of traction, so more people became aware that I was appearing on the show. But I was blown away by all the messages and support."

stories.summary: "A study from about 10 years ago shows that we have, roughly, 30 trillion cells in our body - if you're an adult human," says Dr Freeman. "But we have about 38 trillion microbial cells. So it's about one to one." Simply put, microbial cells are building blocks of microorganisms - living things that are too small to be seen with the naked eye. While some live on our skin, the vast majority live in our large intestine. While it may be unsettling to think about, these tiny cells are mostly doing our body a lot of good - helping to modulate our immune system and protecting our skin and gut barriers. However, those cells don't stay put. In fact, microbes are continuously shed from the human body into the surrounding environment, leaving a type of fingerprint behind. Looking into the unique nature of these cells, a study at the University of Chicago followed seven families over six weeks - three of whom moved home during that period. "Each family had a distinct signature of the microbes," Dr Freeman says of the results. "All the people in the family shared it. They populated the house as soon as they were in it. Even pets had an influence in it in that the pets and owners shared this signature."

stories.title: CUH criticised by HSE for 'conducting business via media'
stories.summary: The Chief Executive of the HSE has criticised Cork University Hospital (CUH) for highlighting issues at the facility through the media. Controversy has surrounded the hospital since its CEO Jennifer Kearney told the HSE in August that a shortfall of around 1,000 staff meant the hospital would not be safe going into winter. However, HSE CEO Anne O'Connor is to criticise CUH for how it has conducted its "management business" when she appears before the Oireachtas Health Committee later today. "As a hospital, CUH is not unique in facing huge service pressures. But it is unique in that it appears to be conducting its management business via the media with extraordinary regularity," she will tell TDs and Senators. "We need to change the working environment [at CUH] that has been created recently so we can engage respectfully and professionally and work together through the coming months for the benefit of the patients that we serve," her opening statement reads. Opposition politicians and medics at CUH have called for an independent assessment of staffing levels at the facility, which is in Taoiseach Micheál Martin's Cork South-Central Dáil constituency.

stories.title: UK inflation rises to 1-year high, markets trim rate bets
stories.summary: British annual inflation rose to a one-year high of 3.6% in October from 3.5% in September, official figures showed today, but investors trimmed bets on a Bank of England rate rise next month as some underlying components held steady. The increase in the headline rate of inflation was in line with the median expectation of economists in a Reuters poll but less than the increase to 3.7% which the Bank of England forecast this month when it raised interest rates for the first time in three years. Two underlying measures of inflation - core inflation and services price inflation - held steady where economists had forecast they would rise. "Today's slightly softer headline inflation data make a December interest rate hike less likely, but it does little to change the broader outlook," David Rees, chief economist at fund manager Schroders, said. The Bank of England sees nearly 5% inflation in the second quarter of 2027 due to higher energy prices caused by the Iran war. Markets saw a slightly lower chance of a rate hike next month - at 80% rather than 90% - but they still expect three or four quarter-point hikes between now and the end of next year. Higher fuel prices and an increase in tobacco taxes - which came earlier this year than in 2025 - were the main factors pushing inflation higher in October, the Office for National Statistics said.

stories.title: Parrott: I'm now at the level I always knew I could reach
stories.summary: The Republic Of Ireland's red-hot striker Troy Parrott insists he always believed he would get to the level he has attained in an Ireland jersey in this past year as his meteoric rise on the international stage continues. The Real Betis player drilled home two penalty kicks in Ireland's 3-0 win over Kosovo making him only the second Irish player - after Robbie Keane - to score seven international goals in a calendar year. "Professional football is probably one of the hardest professions to make it in," Parrott said when asked about his journey from Tottenham Hotspur to Betis with several stops in between. "There's so many people that want to be a footballer, and I think if I hadn't got maybe a stronger mentality, I could've failed, yeah. "But now I'm at the level where I always thought I could get to. I think there's more levels to go. And I'm really excited about it. "Growing up watching Robbie Keane, he was the main man growing up. It's always what I wanted to do.

stories.title: David Ireland to A Raisin in the Sun - Gate launches 2027 season
stories.summary: The Gate Theatre has announced five productions for its 2027 programme, featuring new work, Irish classics, international plays and the return of an Oscar-nominated Irish star to the Gate stage. The season, themed around "the unspeakable and the unspoken", will include the world premiere of End Times by David Ireland, the European debut of U.S. playwright Amy Herzog's Mary Jane and a new staging of Brian Friel’s Philadelphia, Here I Come!. Opening in February, End Times follows a successful Belfast actor preparing for a BBC interview about his father’s murder during the Troubles. Directed by Katie Posner of British theatre company Paines Plough, it's a dark comedy exploring the impact of historical and personal trauma from the acclaimed author of Cyprus Avenue and Ulster American. The Gate's summer production for 2027 will see Artistic Director Roisin McBrinn directing a revival of Philadelphia, Here I Come!, which first premiered as a Gate production in 1964. The programme also includes new productions of George Bernard Shaw's classic Mrs Warren’s Profession, due in April, and African-American playwright Lorraine Hansberry's groundbreaking 1959 work A Raisin in the Sun, to be presented for the 2027 Dublin Theatre Festival. Before the season officially begins, veteran Irish actor Ciarán Hinds returns to the Gate for a short run of Igor Stravinsky's First World War fable The Soldier's Tale in January, blending chamber music, poetry, drama, and movement, and presented as part of the theatre’s ongoing Gatecrashes programme.

stories.title: Bond and Batman: Pattinson is a franchise phenomenon
stories.summary: British actor Robert Pattinson's role as James Bond will cement him as one of Hollywood's most versatile and bankable superstars, but he will have to juggle two of the industry's biggest franchises. The London-born 40-year-old will now be in the incredibly rare position of fronting both the current Batman series - which he started in 2022 - and the new Bond movie. He spent part of this year shooting The Batman: Part II with director Matt Reeves, which is being produced by Warner Bros and is slated to hit screens in February 2028. That could even clash with the release of the Bond reboot by Denis Villeneuve, although no release date has been published by new studio owner Amazon MGM. "I think that might lead to some intense negotiations between the studios down the line, although it's probably manageable given the production cycles for major films like that," Bruce Nash, founder of box office-tracking website The Numbers, told AFP. "Whether the public will embrace someone who is both Batman and Bond is something of an open question, and I can't think of another case of someone owning the role of two such major characters at the same time."

stories.title: Xi and Putin call for free trade ahead of Trump meeting
stories.summary: China's President Xi Jinping has pledged to stand up against trade protectionism, while his Russian counterpart Vladimir Putin criticised Western sanctions as the two set the stage for a high-stakes trilateral meeting with Donald Trump. They delivered their speeches at an Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in the southern Chinese tech hub of Shenzhen, ahead of US President Trump's arrival from Manila, where he was meeting key regional allies. The three men are due to meet on the sidelines tomorrow and potentially discuss Russia's war with Ukraine and the US war in Iran, as well as other flashpoints such as trade, AI and nuclear weapons. The meeting has drawn comparisons with the 1945 Yalta Conference between the US, Britain and the Soviet Union that formalized spheres of influence, set the stage for the post-World War Two order and became shorthand for great-power deals imposed on smaller countries. It has also unnerved leaders of smaller economies, particularly in Europe and Asia, who fear the world's greatest military powers will disregard their interests. In his opening address, Mr Xi urged support for what he called "free and open trade," trying to portray his country as a stable partner on the global stage, in contrast with main economic rival the US, which has raised tariffs and adopted a more muscular foreign policy under Trump.

stories.title: How did Grand Theft Auto become such a big deal?
stories.summary: Analysis: Grand Theft Auto is a cultural phenomenon which has captured the hearts, minds and wallets of gamers everywhere This week, developers at Rockstar Games will finally release Grand Theft Auto VI. The latest installment in the best-selling franchise, it's set to become the most important pop culture release of the year. After all, the last game, 2013’s Grand Theft Auto V, made over $800 million on release day alone and went on to gross in the region of $10 billion, making it the highest grossing piece of popular entertainment in history. The new game is expected to make even more: gaming website Gamespot has valued preorders for Grand Theft Auto VI at a whopping $630 million already. But what is it about Grand Theft Auto that has captured the hearts, minds, and wallets of gamers everywhere? Grand Theft Auto VI looks set to be a game of excess in just about every way. In typical Rockstar fashion, the story is replete with all the trappings of extreme wealth: drugs, drink, and violence. But the excess doesn’t end there. The in-game map is projected to span about 125 kilometers squared. For comparison, the beloved 2011 roleplaying classic Skyrim was set in a region of what now seems a relatively modest 40 kilometers squared. That extreme wealth isn’t just an in-game feature, either. Business Insider estimated the budget for the game in the region of $1.5 billon, which would make this the single most expensive videogame ever produced. Rockstar’s videogames are largely community-driven, packed with small details and larger mysteries. After the release of Red Dead Redemption 2, fans had a lot of fun working together to discover Easter eggs and hidden questlines across a rugged Western landscape, echoing the enthusiasm that sustained Grand Theft Auto V’s popularity. Unravelling these mysteries becomes a collaborative and participatory internet-wide hunt.

stories.title: Egan wants consistency from Ireland after Kosovo victory
stories.summary: John Egan has challenged his Republic of Ireland team-mates to find consistency over the next year, after they secured a Nations League promotion play-off with a 3-0 victory against Kosovo in Dublin. Troy Parrott scored two penalties and Jack Moylan was also on target in Dublin to leapfrog their visitors into second place in Group B3. The win also propelled the Euro 2028 co-hosts into a coveted pot-two seeding for next month's qualifying draw for that competition. It was a positive ending to a turbulent campaign where Ireland's performances didn’t always produce the results that they deserved. Egan, who captained Ireland on the night in place of the suspended Nathan Collins, was buoyed by the result and display against Kosovo and now he wants to see his side perform like that on a more regular basis. "I think the last five games have been of a similar standard. We took the game to the opposition, and we got a really good result.

stories.title: Iran attacks Gulf neighbours after US strike on Qeshm
stories.summary: Gulf countries Kuwait and Bahrain said they intercepted missiles and drones from Iran and its Houthi allies in Yemen, after the United States ⁠had struck Qeshm Island in the Strait of Hormuz in an uptick of hostilities despite efforts to end the nine-month-old war. The back-and-forth attacks were a reminder of the hurdles facing diplomatic efforts to end a war that has destabilised the Middle East, pushed up global energy prices and helped fuel the US voter anger that punished US President Donald Trump's Republican Party in the November midterm elections. The Iranian army said it had targeted US drone and missile installations at Kuwait's Ali Al Salem base, after the US ally said its air defences were countering hostile drone attacks. It was the first Iranian attack on the oil-rich country since September. Neighbouring Bahrain said it had intercepted Iranian aerial attacks for the third time this week. It accused Tehran of maintaining a "systematic hostile approach" of targeting the country, which hosts the US Navy's Fifth Fleet.

stories.title: Extra-time heartache for Ireland U21s in Euros play-off
stories.summary: Republic of Ireland 2 Finland 2 (AET, Finland win 3-2 on aggregate) Ireland missed out on European U21 Championship qualification in gut-wrenching fashion as 10-man Finland claimed an extra-time winner in front of 5,177 spectators at Turner’s Cross. The Boys in Green had flipped the first-leg deficit as Trent Kone-Doherty and hometown favourite Leon Ayinde bagged second-half goals, but a late penalty allowed away captain Matias Siltanen to force extra-time. Ireland gained an extra man as Miska Ylitolva was sent off just before the final whistle, only for the Finns to claim the ticket to next summer’s finals thanks to substitute Lauri Laine’s 110th-minute strike. Having lost a penalty shoot-out to Israel in the 2022 play-offs and missed out on the 2024 play-offs on a head-to-head tiebreaker with Norway, this was yet another heartbreaking close call. Jim Crawford made two changes from the 1-0 defeat in Finland. Empoli’s Matteo Egan was handed his first start at right wing-back, while Kone-Doherty was enlisted on the left flank.

stories.title: Gamers count down the hours to Grand Theft Auto VI
stories.summary: Grand Theft Auto fans are eagerly awaiting tonight's release of the latest instalment in the blockbuster video game series, 13 years after its predecessor. Rockstar Games' hugely successful franchise first launched almost three decades ago and is known for its open-world gameplay, car thefts, police chases and criminal mayhem. Grand Theft Auto VI (GTA VI), the 17th instalment of the series, is expected to be one of the biggest gaming launches of 2026, with fans going to extreme lengths to prepare for its arrival. But what makes the franchise so popular? Here is everything you need to know about the video game ahead of its highly anticipated release at 12am Thursday. The franchise began in 1997 as a relatively simple, top-down game that allowed players to roam fictional cities, steal vehicles, evade police and commit crimes. A sequel was released two years later. But the release of Grand Theft Auto III in 2001 helped redefine open-world gaming, giving players greater freedom to explore a three-dimensional city, complete missions and interact with their surroundings.

stories.title: Player ratings: Moylan stars as Ireland cruise to second
stories.summary: The Republic of Ireland coasted past Kosovo on Tuesday at the Aviva Stadium to finish second in their UEFA Nations League B group. Ireland's player of the match away to Austria on Saturday, Kelleher had a much quieter night here but it was still a calm and assured display when needed. He was at full stretch when seeing out Lindon Emerllahu’s early drive, showed good hands to deal with a Vedat Muriqi effort and got down well to steer Ilir Krasniqi’s header to safety before half-time. Playing against 10-men, Ireland kicked on after the break and kept attacking, allowing Kelleher to enjoy a comfortable, stress-free half as a result. Heimir Hallgrimsson had flagged that Abankwah was battling cramp following Saturday’s narrow defeat in Austria but the Udinese man was passed fit to fill the right wing-back role again. He had licence to push forward and while he put in an honest shift, there was no edge-of-the-seat chemistry with Jack Moylan on that right side of the pitch when Ireland were attacking. It was functional and he covered the ground down that side, defending well when needed and nearly scored in the opening minutes of the second-half. stories.title: Churches to be lit red to highlight Christian persecution
stories.summary: Churches and state buildings will be lit red this evening to remind people of the continuing global persecution of Christians. Over 413 million Christians live in countries where serious violations of religious freedom occur, and around 220m Christians worldwide are directly exposed to persecution. The issue is worsening due to extremist violence, authoritarian governments and religious nationalism, according to Aid to the Church in Need (ACN). A report by the pontifical foundation has found that conditions for Christians have worsened in more than half of 18 countries examined. The study, which covers the period from August 2024 to June 2026, examines countries where religious freedom violations affecting Christians are considered particularly concerning. In many cases, the report found that persecution had intensified in specific regions, rather than at a national level.

stories.title: Moylan savours special night as Ireland beat Kosovo
stories.summary: Jack Moylan scored a goal and was named player of the match in a match he described as "one of my favourite games ever", after the Republic beat Kosovo 3-0 in the Nations League. Moylan's goal and two from Troy Parrott fired Ireland into a Nations League play-off berth, as they finished second in Group B. The result ensured that Heimir Hallgrimsson's side finished runners-up in group B3, and also propelled the Euro 2028 co-hosts into a coveted pot-two seeding for next month's qualifying draw for that competition. The game turned on a penalty in the 26th minute when Kreshnik Hajrizi was sent off for handling the ball off the line, and Parrott took advantage with a top-corner finish. A further penalty from Parrott and a wonderfully placed second-half header from Moylan ensured that Ireland ended an often turbulent Nations League campaign on a high. The development and growth of Moylan in the Ireland squad has been one of the highlights of the campaign and, once again, he ran the show for Ireland at the Aviva Stadium.

stories.title: Hit-and-run jail sentence 'an insult' to nurse's memory
stories.summary: The family of a nurse who was killed in a hit-and-run in Co Limerick earlier this year has said the sentence imposed on the 19-year-old man who caused the crash was "outrageously lenient" and an insult to her memory. Keelan O'Connell, of Scanlon Park, Castleconnell, has been jailed for four years and 11 months after being convicted of eight offences including dangerous driving causing the death of Áine O'Reilly. The three-car collision happened on the N24 at Grange West, Boher on 13 February. The 33-year-old nurse was driving to work at Shannondoc in Limerick for a night shift when she was killed. Speaking outside Limerick Circuit Court this afternoon, Ms O'Reilly's brother Conor said the court had an opportunity today to show that the roads belong to hard-working, honest citizens rather than thugs or bullies. "The courts are in place to protect us all. We have lost a sister, a daughter and a beautiful human being with a bright future ahead of her, which we feel has not been reflected in today's sentencing which was outrageously lenient.

stories.summary: Around 40 data breach notifications from credit unions have been reported to the Data Protection Commission (DPC), it is understood. stories.summary: Troy Parrott proved to be a November hero once again for the Republic of Ireland as his brace of penalties and a Jack Moylan goal saw off ten-man Kosovo at Aviva Stadium, securing the tangible rewards that come with a top two finish in their UEFA Nations League group. Heimir Hallgrimsson's side will now take their place in the promotion/relegation play-off draw which will be held this Friday, 20 November, and crucially will also be in pot two for the Euro 2028 qualifying draw on 6 December - the latter boosting hopes that the Boys in Green will grace Aviva Stadium on the major tournament stage. As a sign of how satisfied he was by the performance in Saturday's defeat in Linz, Hallgrimsson opted to make just one enforced alteration as the experienced John Egan came into the side in place of injured captain Nathan Collins. Kosovo, meanwhile, were shorn of a number of key players through injury and suspension including Juventus’ Edon Zhegrova. But imposing target man and record goalscorer Vedat Muriqi, who scored the winner two months ago in Pristina, led their line as captain.

stories.title: Mother of injured girl 'relieved' at Bouchaker sentence
stories.summary: The mother of the young girl who was seriously injured in the Parnell Square attack has said she is "relieved" at the life sentence handed down to Riad Bouchaker, adding that "a life sentence for a life sentence" was fair. Bouchaker was sentenced to life in prison yesterday for the attempted murder of three children. He was also convicted of stabbing childcare worker Leanne Flynn and assaulting two other children and a teenager on 23 November 2023. The attack sparked riots on the streets of Dublin that evening. Posting online this afternoon, the mother thanked those who supported her and her daughter since that day, adding however that it was "still painful" to hear of the events of that day put into words. Her five-year-old daughter was the most seriously injured in the attacks and has been left with a severe, life-long brain injury after Bouchaker stabbed her in the heart. "I was asked if I was happy with the sentencing. I am relieved. I don't think happy is an emotion I associate with that day in 2023.

stories.title: Rooney joined army 'to make his dad proud', inquest hears
stories.summary: The mother of Private Seán Rooney has told an inquest that his death has "destroyed" her and her family's lives. The 24-year-old, from Newtowncunningham in Co Donegal, was killed during a United Nations peacekeeping mission in Lebanon on 14 December 2022. Delivering a pen portrait, on the first day of the inquest, Natasha McCloskey said that he was her firstborn and only son. She said that he was loved and cherished by his extended family and "was a loving, kind, caring and empathetic person, someone who brought joy to everyone around him". Ms McCloskey told the jury at Dublin District Coroner's Court that her son had lost his father when he was 10 years old. He was also a solider and she believed this was one of the reasons that he chose to join the army, adding that "because he wanted to make his dad proud".

stories.title: Erasmus handed six-match suspension over comments
stories.summary: South Africa head coach Rassie Erasmus has been suspended for six international matches by World Rugby, starting with this Saturday's Nations Championship clash with Ireland at Aviva Stadium. The punishment stems from a World Rugby review into comments made by Erasmus concerning officiating during the Springboks’ Nations Championship match against France last Friday. He had been speaking to the media at a press conference in Dublin yesterday. An independent panel imposed the sanction under World Rugby's Match Official Abuse Sanction Process. The punishment includes any matchday involvement including coaching, direct or indirect contact with team management or players on matchdays. He will not be allowed enter the stadium. It was later confirmed that SA Rugby will be requesting a full misconduct hearing for Springbok coach Rassie Erasmus following the sanctioning.

stories.title: Bowes' nationality irrelevant to EU sanctions - McEntee
stories.summary: Minister for Foreign Affairs Helen McEntee has said the nationality of Irish journalist Chay Bowes was irrelevant when it came to him being sanctioned by the EU for acting as a propagandist for the Russian government. The listing was announced by EU foreign ministers at a meeting in Brussels yesterday. He was one of 113 people and entities listed by EU foreign ministers in connection with Russia's ongoing war against Ukraine. Speaking in Brussels today, Minister McEntee said: "Nobody is above the law. There are clear rules, and proposals, and procedures in place when it comes to sanctions. "It doesn't matter where they're from. If you meet that criteria and you're put on a sanctions list, then we're going to support that. "Nationality for us doesn't come into it, and it sends a very clear message that those who want to engage in propaganda, who want to support Russia and its war machine, and the almost five years of brutal aggression against Ukraine - but now also against other member states - then this is the type of response they'll get."

stories.summary: Australian racehorse trainer Bjorn Baker expressed his distress after the remains of his former Melbourne Cup runner So You Are were discovered in a skip. So You Are, ⁠which ran eighth at this month's Melbourne Cup, was euthanised after falling ill with a severe bout of colic and undergoing emergency surgery, Baker said in a statement on Monday. Footage subsequently emerged on social media showing the horse's remains in a skip at a Sydney waste facility. "Like everyone who has seen the footage, I am deeply distressed by the handling of So You Are's remains," said Baker. "He ‌was a much-loved horse, and ⁠he deserved to be treated with dignity and respect after his death." REC Equine Specialists, which operated on the horse before its death, apologised for the incident, saying it had ceased using a contractor that collected the horse for disposal at a licensed landfill.
